name: Accessibility in Every Classroom
title: Accessibility in Every Classroom
answer: Accessibility tools such as live captions, text to speech, dictation and image descriptions can support every student, not only students with disabilities, and offering them to everyone means students who need them do not stand out. The choice of when to use a support is a decision for the student's team, because a tool should remove the barrier to access while the student still builds the skills the lesson targets. AI output is not automatically accessible, so teachers must prompt for plain language and check the results.

sections.body: This idea is that accessibility supports have moved from being special arrangements for a few students to everyday tools that help a whole class. Live captions assist students who are deaf or hard of hearing, and they also assist English learners and anyone working in a noisy room. Text to speech and dictation serve students with reading or writing disabilities and many other students as well. When these tools are simply available to everyone, the students who depend on them avoid being singled out. The problem it solves is the stigma and separation that come with supports that are reserved for a labelled group.
sections.heading: The idea

sections.body: In a classroom, the tools are switched on for the whole group rather than handed to named students. Live captions run in Microsoft PowerPoint and Teams, and text to speech or dictation is available through Microsoft Immersive Reader or Read&Write by Texthelp. The text gives the example of a student with dyslexia using text to speech in history class to open up the content, while in a reading lesson the IEP team decides whether and how that student should use it. Image descriptions open visual content to students who are blind or have low vision, and teachers can write alternative text for images in their own materials, using AI to draft descriptions they then check. The text does not set out separate grade bands, so the same approach applies across year levels with the level of independence adjusted by the team.
sections.heading: How it works in school

sections.body: The text reports a study of quiz questions generated by AI for students who are deaf or hard of hearing, which found frequent compound sentences, double negatives and complex clauses (Chen et al., 2026). Teachers in that work had to prompt specifically for plain language and then check the results, which supports the book's point that accessible does not happen automatically. The text also refers to researchers describing strategic offloading, where a tool handles the part of a task that blocks access while the student still builds the skills the lesson targets (Seung & Basham, 2026). No other studies or figures are given for this idea.
sections.heading: What the evidence says

sections.body: The main limit is that AI output cannot be trusted to be accessible on its own, so a teacher has to ask for plain language and verify what comes back. The decision about when a support is used stays with people, and in the case of a student with dyslexia the IEP team decides whether and how text to speech is used in a reading lesson, even though the same tool is fine for opening content in history. Tool choice also carries conditions, since Be My Eyes requires users to be at least 17 and so suits staff and older students only, while Microsoft Seeing AI is free. Teachers who use AI to draft image descriptions remain responsible for checking them. These are practice points, not legal advice.
